title: [Advanced Admin] New page: Recovering a compromised WordPress site
body:
## What is the new page you are requesting?

A page in the Advanced Administration Handbook, under Security, on responding to a known or suspected compromise. It would cover what an administrator or host does after a breach, for example:

- Confirming the compromise and preserving evidence (logs, a copy of the files and database) before cleaning up.
- Restoring from a known-good backup versus cleaning in place.
- Replacing WordPress core, plugins and themes with clean copies (for example with `wp core verify-checksums` and `wp plugin verify-checksums`).
- Checking for unknown administrator accounts, unexpected must-use plugins, and modified `wp-config.php` or `.htaccess` files.
- Rotating credentials: WordPress passwords, application passwords, the salts in `wp-config.php`, database, SFTP and hosting accounts.
- Getting blocklist warnings removed after cleanup.
- When to involve the hosting provider.

The end-user side could then shrink to a short, non-technical page: signs that a site may be hacked, who to contact, and a link to this handbook page.

## How will this new page help you?

There is no current guidance to link to when a site is compromised. I ran into this while working on the password reset docs (#1707, #79). The natural last step after a password reset is "if the account was compromised, a new password is not enough". But there is nowhere good to send the reader:

- The Advanced Administration Handbook has no page on breach response. [Hardening WordPress](https://developer.wordpress.org/advanced-administration/security/hardening/) covers prevention, not recovery.
- [FAQ My site was hacked](https://wordpress.org/documentation/article/faq-my-site-was-hacked/) in the end-user docs is mostly links to external blog posts from 2008 to 2013. Several are on plain `http://` URLs, and it recommends specific vendors and services. #369 already noted that most of these links do not meet the [external linking policy](https://make.wordpress.org/docs/handbook/documentation-team-handbook/external-linking-policy/). Recent fixes (#1963) only patched a single broken link.

This page is also listed in #426 (FAQ content review: keep, move to DevHub, or delete). This issue proposes the "move" outcome for the technical part, with a page written from scratch rather than migrated as-is.

title: [DevHub] WP_Query::get_posts use case clarification

labels.name: developer documentation (DevHub)
labels.description: Improvements or additions to developer documentation

body:
<!--
Please fill out the following sections with as many details as you can.
We can't work on fixing an issue unless we have all the details. 
So please be sure your submission is complete; if it's not, it will be marked as incomplete, and closed without being fixed.

-->

## Issue Description

I've encountered a pretty gnarly issue a few times with my (incorrect) usage of `WP_Query::get_posts()` which can be quite tricky to debug.

Essentially, `new WP_Query($args)->get_posts()` can silently corrupt `tax_query` results due to core code that writes the first taxonomy and term to `query_vars['taxonomy']` and `query_vars['term']` which then effects the SQL generated when `WP_Query::get_posts()` runs the query for the second time.

This causes incorrect results particularly when you're trying to do a `tax_query` with multiple taxonomies and term arrays with `'relation' => 'AND'` and `'operator' => 'IN'` - (for example, if you're using `wp_query` to build faceted search interfaces). The first taxonomy and term end up appended as a new separate clause with a single term, even if that taxonomy had multiple terms in the originally passed arguments.

I don't really think this is a bug, its more an issue of me not realising that `WP_Query::get_posts()` should only ever be used internally and *should never* be used to get results from the already constructed `WP_Query` object.

The documentation page for `WP_Query::get_posts()` is usually going to be the first result if you google something like "get posts from a wp_query", the method name can be easily misconstrued as a simple getter, and the documentation is minimal.

## URL of the Page with the Issue

[https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/classes/wp_query/get_posts/](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/classes/wp_query/get_posts/)

## Section of Page with the issue

Description

## Why is this a problem?

Its perfectly reasonable for a developer to end up on this documentation page when looking up how to get the _results_ from an already constructed WP_Query and incorrectly assume that this method is what they want. In lots of cases, this would lead to that developer using `->get_posts()` instead of `->posts`. This will often be missed, since get_posts will re-run the query and often produce the same results, however it is inefficient because they would essentially be running the query twice, and it can produce unexpected silent failures in complex tax_queries as described above in the Issue Description.

## Suggested Fix

I think the fix is a one line documentation change:

"Note: This method is used internally by WP_Query and should not be used to retrieve post results from an already instantiated WP_Query object. To get the array of post results from a WP_Query, you should use `->posts` instead"

title: [DevHub] Update wp_verify_nonce example to unslash and sanitize input

labels.name: developer documentation (DevHub)
labels.description: Improvements or additions to developer documentation

body:
## Issue Description
The documentation example for `wp_verify_nonce()` shows a nonce value being read directly from `$_POST`. Since `$_POST` contains user-supplied data, the example should follow WordPress coding standards and security recommendations by **unslashing** and **sanitizing** the value before using it.

## URL of the Page with the Issue
[https://developer.wordpress.org/apis/security/nonces/](https://developer.wordpress.org/apis/security/nonces/)

## Section of Page with the issue
[Verifying a nonce passed in an AJAX request](https://developer.wordpress.org/apis/security/nonces/#verifying-a-nonce-passed-in-an-ajax-request)

## Why is this a problem?
The example code that demonstrates nonce verification accesses `$_POST['my_nonce']` directly:

`wp_verify_nonce( $_POST['my_nonce'], 'process-comment' . $comment_id );`

This does not follow current WordPress coding standards and security recommendations, which advise sanitizing and unslashing user input before use.
Developers often copy examples from the documentation verbatim, so showing direct access to $_POST may unintentionally encourage unsafe patterns.

## Suggested Fix
Sanitizing and unslashing user input before use. 
Suggested update:

`wp_verify_nonce( sanitize_text_field( wp_unslash( $_POST['my_nonce'] ) ), 'process-comment' . $comment_id );`

title: Settings pages: register_setting() does not create an option, get_option() $default_value, and {$wpdb->prefix}_options typo
body:
## Issue Description
Three small errors across the Settings pages of the Plugin Handbook:

1. **Using Settings API → Adding Settings** says `register_setting()` "will create an entry in the `{$wpdb->prefix}_options` table". It does not. `register_setting()` (`src/wp-includes/option.php:3076-3172`) only adds the option to the allowed list, adds the `sanitize_option_{$option_name}` / `default_option_{$option_name}` filters, fires `register_setting` and stores the args in `$wp_registered_settings`. It never calls `add_option()` or `update_option()`. The row is written later, when the settings form is saved (`src/wp-admin/options.php:351` calls `update_option()`, which falls back to `add_option()` at `src/wp-includes/option.php:929`). Checked on WordPress 7.1.4: right after `register_setting( 'reading', $name )`, `wp_options` has 0 rows for `$name` and `get_option( $name )` returns `false`.
2. **Using Settings API → Getting Settings** shows the second parameter of `get_option()` as `$default`. Core names it `$default_value` (`src/wp-includes/option.php:78`: `function get_option( $option, $default_value = false )`), and so does the reference page.
3. The options table is written as `{$wpdb->prefix}_options`, with an extra underscore. `$wpdb` builds table names as prefix plus name with nothing between (`src/wp-includes/class-wpdb.php:1180`: `$blog_prefix . $table`), and the prefix already ends in `_`. On a default install `{$wpdb->prefix}_options` gives `wp__options`; the real table is `wp_options` (`$wpdb->options`). The same typo is on three pages:
   - https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/settings/using-settings-api/#adding-settings
   - https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/settings/options-api/#where-options-are-stored
   - https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-basics/uninstall-methods/ (deactivation vs. uninstall table, row "Remove Options from …")

## URL of the Page with the Issue
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/settings/using-settings-api/
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/settings/options-api/
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-basics/uninstall-methods/

## Section of Page with the issue
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/settings/using-settings-api/#adding-settings
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/settings/using-settings-api/#getting-settings
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/settings/options-api/#where-options-are-stored
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-basics/uninstall-methods/ (table above "Method 1")

## Why is this a problem?
A reader who believes `register_setting()` creates the row expects `get_option()` to return a stored value before the form was ever saved, and gets `false` (or the registered default) instead. The `$default` name no longer matches core or the reference page. Copying `{$wpdb->prefix}_options` into a query targets a table that does not exist.

## Suggested Fix
**Using Settings API → Adding Settings**, current text:

> You must define a new setting using `register_setting()`, it will create an entry in the `{$wpdb->prefix}_options` table.

Replace with:

> You must define a new setting using [`register_setting()`](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/register_setting/). This registers the setting with WordPress; the value is stored in the `{$wpdb->prefix}options` table the first time the settings form is saved.

**Using Settings API → Getting Settings**, current code:

```php
get_option(
    string $option,
    mixed $default = false
);
```

Replace with:

```php
get_option(
    string $option,
    mixed $default_value = false
);
```

**Options API → Where Options are Stored?**, current text:

> Options are stored in the `{$wpdb->prefix}_options` table. `$wpdb->prefix` is defined by the `$table_prefix` variable set in the `wp-config.php` file.

Replace with:

> Options are stored in the `{$wpdb->prefix}options` table (available as `$wpdb->options`). `$wpdb->prefix` is defined by the `$table_prefix` variable set in the `wp-config.php` file.

**Uninstall Methods**, table row, current text:

> Remove Options from {$wpdb->prefix}_options

Replace with:

> Remove Options from {$wpdb->prefix}options

title: Working with Custom Taxonomies: is_taxonomy is deprecated, and there is no archive at /course/
body:
## Issue Description
Two statements on this page do not match current core:

1. **Using Your Taxonomy** lists `is_taxonomy`. That function is deprecated since WordPress 3.0.0 and only forwards to `taxonomy_exists()` (`src/wp-includes/deprecated.php:2507, 2513-2515`: `@deprecated 3.0.0 Use taxonomy_exists()`, then `_deprecated_function( __FUNCTION__, '3.0.0', 'taxonomy_exists()' )`). The current function is `taxonomy_exists()` (`src/wp-includes/taxonomy.php:384`).
2. **Summary** says the example creates an archive page at `/course/`. Core only registers the `{slug}/%course%` permastruct for a taxonomy (`src/wp-includes/class-wp-taxonomy.php:512-513`), so there are per-term archives at `/course/{term-slug}/`, but no rule for `/course/` itself. With the page's example registered on WordPress 7.1.4 (`/%postname%/` permalinks), `/course/math/` matches `course/([^/]+)/?$ => index.php?course=$1`, while `/course/` falls through to the generic page rule `index.php?pagename=course`, which is a 404 unless a page with that slug exists.

Related open issue for the same page: #827 (add `show_in_rest` to the example).

## URL of the Page with the Issue
https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/taxonomies/working-with-custom-taxonomies/

## Section of Page with the issue
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/taxonomies/working-with-custom-taxonomies/#summary
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/taxonomies/working-with-custom-taxonomies/#using-your-taxonomy

## Why is this a problem?
Calling `is_taxonomy()` triggers a deprecation notice with `WP_DEBUG` on, so code copied from the handbook starts out deprecated. The archive sentence sends readers to a URL that returns a 404, so they think their taxonomy or permalinks are broken.

## Suggested Fix
**Summary**, current text:

> With our Courses Taxonomy example, WordPress will automatically create an archive page and child pages for the `course` Taxonomy.
>
> The archive page will be at `/course/` with child pages spawning under it using the Term's slug (`/course/%%term-slug%%/`).

Replace with:

> With our Courses Taxonomy example, WordPress will automatically create an archive page for each term in the `course` Taxonomy.
>
> Each term archive uses the Term's slug, for example `/course/%%term-slug%%/`. WordPress does not create a page at `/course/` itself; that URL returns a 404 unless you add something there, such as a page with the slug `course`.

**Using Your Taxonomy**, current text:

> - `is_taxonomy`: Allows you to determine if a given taxonomy exists.

Replace with:

> - [`taxonomy_exists()`](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/taxonomy_exists/): Allows you to determine if a given taxonomy exists.

title: New page: `WP_SECRETS_KEY` (WordPress 7.2)
body:
WordPress 7.2 adds the Secrets API ([#66187](https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/66187)), which encrypts credentials that plugins store, such as API keys, under a key from a new `wp-config.php` constant, `WP_SECRETS_KEY`. Site Health will tell site owners to add this key, and we'd like to link it to a page that explains it ([#66380 comment:9](https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/66380#comment:9)). This could be a HelpHub page, or a section on the wp-config.php page in the Advanced Administration Handbook, whichever fits better. It needs a stable URL.

What the page should cover:

- **What it is:** the key that encrypts secrets stored by WordPress and plugins. Without it, plugins can't use the Secrets API.
- **How to add it:** one line in `wp-config.php`, above "That's all, stop editing!", with a base64-encoded 32-byte random value. Site Health shows a ready-made line, and new installs get one automatically.
- **Back it up with your database:** a database backup without the key can't decrypt the secrets in it.
- **Never change it once secrets are stored.** Unlike the keys and salts, changing or removing it makes every stored secret unreadable until the old value is restored. Rotating the salts doesn't affect it.
- **Hosts** can define it for every site they run. A host or plugin that manages keys elsewhere, such as a key management service, may not need it at all. Site Health says so.
- **Multisite:** one key in `wp-config.php` covers the whole network.

The technical background and a full reference are at https://secretsapi.dev/. I'm happy to review a draft or write the first one.

title: Sub-Menus: outdated add_submenu_page() signature and a wrong add_options_page() parent slug
body:
## Issue Description
The **Add a Sub-Menu** section shows an old signature for `add_submenu_page()`. It ends with `callable $function = ''`. The current core signature is:

`add_submenu_page( $parent_slug, $page_title, $menu_title, $capability, $menu_slug, $callback = '', $position = null )`

The callback parameter is named `$callback`, and `$position` was added in WordPress 5.3 (`@since 5.3.0 Added the $position parameter.` in `wp-admin/includes/plugin.php`).

The **Predefined Sub-Menus** list also has two errors:
- `add_options_page()` is listed twice, once with `options-general.php` and once with `settings.php`. `add_options_page()` always uses `options-general.php`. `settings.php` is the Network Admin parent, which already has its own line at the end of the list.
- In the page source, the `add_users_page()` link starts with `hhttps://` instead of `https://`. The rendered page on developer.wordpress.org shows a working link, but the Markdown source is wrong.

## URL of the Page with the Issue
https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/administration-menus/sub-menus/

## Section of Page with the issue
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/administration-menus/sub-menus/#add-a-sub-menu (signature)
- https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/administration-menus/sub-menus/#predefined-sub-menus (helper function list)

## Why is this a problem?
Developers do not learn about `$position` from this page, and the parameter name does not match the function reference. The duplicate `add_options_page()` line tells them the helper adds a page under `settings.php`, which it never does.

## Suggested Fix
- Signature: `callable $function = ''` → `callable $callback = '',` followed by `int|float $position = null`
- Remove the `add_options_page()` – `settings.php` line
- `hhttps://` → `https://` in the `add_users_page()` link

The AJAX handler examples call `sanitize_post_title( $title )` before saving the value with `update_user_meta()`. `sanitize_post_title( $title )` → `sanitize_text_field( $title )` in all three places. [`sanitize_text_field()`](https://developer.wordpress.org/reference/functions/sanitize_text_field/) is the core function for a plain text value from user input (`wp-includes/formatting.php`).

body:
In the Make Docs sidebar there are links to the upcoming meetings, with descriptions, times and dates.

However, this can be easily overlooked, or takes multiple steps to add to your calendar.

We could have a GitHub Action to automatically create `.ics` files so users can import the upcoming meetings to their calendar. 

**Finished deliverable**
- one `.ics` import for all meetings (import)
- one for individual dates (import)
- represented as icons in the [Make Docs sidebar](make.wordpress.org/docs)
- a separate functionality piece in the action script to determine when the next script should be run (generate new `.ics` links)

**Script parameters**
- Meeting Time and Date (GMT)
- Meeting Name
- Meeting Notes (post body)

One caveat or potential benefit, is that calendars will automatically translate the time to the timezone the contributor is currently in. 

In the past, I have missed meetings because of Daylight Savings Time, which does not exist in all timezones. I am hopeful that with this script, the dates and times will be imported to the _right_ time, regardless of the contributor's timezone.

**QA:** If the action works correctly, it saves a step of having to figure out what the "Time Is" in your locale vs. the meeting time in the sidebar.

labels.name: developer documentation (DevHub)
labels.description: Improvements or additions to developer documentation

body:
## Status Quo
Currently the https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-basics/best-practices/ page suggests a couple Plugin Boilerplates as starting points for aspiring (or experienced) DEVs to create Plugins.
See section [Boilerplate Plugins](https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-basics/best-practices/#boilerplate-starting-points).
All of them are very good starting points, but all of them unless the WP CLI one are _very old_ and _never been updated since_.
Some are last updated 2014, others 9 years ago.

## URL of the Page with the Issue
https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-basics/best-practices/

## Section of Page with the issue
https://developer.wordpress.org/plugins/plugin-basics/best-practices/#boilerplate-starting-points

## Why is this a problem?
It is not the best to start _new_ development with code that was written 9 years ago (even if it still works). 
There have not been any updates to those libraries since. 
This basally encourages "non-evolution" and suggests to _new_, aspiring devs (but also existing experienced devs) to simply go on forever with the same old code that "worked once, still works, so why not".

While this is OK, it would be better to also provide a link to a _maintained_ and actively developed boilerplate that adjusted some of the code to newer approaches and as well (and most importantly) commits to continue to develop the boilerplate and listens to the community requests and accepts PRs. 
None of the currently suggested boilerplate has accepted a single PR since years, despite numerous valid PRs by users to the respective repos. All of the suggested boilerplates are as said being developed many years ago and never evolved from that. Meanwhile, we have autoloaders, PHP evolved, WordPress evolved. So definitely, it would be a good time to add a link to a more maintained, developed Boilerplate.

## Suggested Fix
Such boilerplate [does exist](https://github.com/TukuToi/better-wp-plugin-boilerplate). It is actively maintained, developed, accepts PRs and attempts to _evolve_, rather than stay stuck on what worked once (and may work forever or not).
It does not yet include _all_ new things we could include, but that is partially also the reason why I suggest listing it on the page. The more users are aware of it the more users will contribute and the more the boilerplate can be evolving.
It is certainly more up to date than the other linked boilerplates, and is _actively maintained_, and accepts/listens to community input (something that has been completely lacking from the other boilerplates)

body:
This issue was originally created as [HelpHub #333](https://github.com/WordPress/HelpHub/issues/333) by atachibana and comment was added by [ashfame](https://github.com/ashfame).

---
There are two methods:
1. Using the plugin
2. Setting up WordPress manually (without plugin)

For above method 2, the step will be (but might be missing)
1. Backup WordPress files and database
2. Set SSL certificate
3. Change WordPress URL from Administration Screen
4. Replace the string 'http' to 'https' in the database contents
5. Add redirect code into .htaccess

---
## Comment by [ashfame](https://github.com/ashfame)

I just switched an old site to refresh up my memory for the exact steps:

#### Actual Instructions

- Take a backup of files and database in case you need to revert for whatever reasons.
- Get your webhost to install a TLS (also referred to as SSL) certificate for your website
- Once installed ensure that your website is accessible on `https` URL, by simply replacing `http` with `https` i.e. adding a `s` to it. Eg: If your website was `http://www.domain.com`, new URL would be `https://www.domain.com`
- See if you have any errors in your browser console complaining about mixed content, as you browse different pages on your website. Usually when using good quality plugin and theme, there won't be an issue. But if you do, you will need to resolve these issues.
- Once you are satisfied with the results and are ready to flip the switch, go ahead and update the website URL in WordPress admin: `Settings` > `General`.
- Now if you try to access http version of your website you will be redirected to https version. Best to try in an incognito/private window in your browser to test this.

#### Potential issues:

> `http` to `https` redirect isn't working

I am not sure if changing the URL in WordPress causes it to issue redirects, though I believe it does. I never use it, as I always handle redirects on a server level.

> Mixed-content warnings

Depending on what resources are causing these errors, it can either be your theme, any plugin you use or actual content you load in post/page and requires a different approach for each one of them.

Post/page content requires you to replace string, can be done via this plugin https://wordpress.org/plugins/better-search-replace/

Theme/plugins would require using the right functions to generate URLs or simply update the hardcoded urls to be https.

## Border settings
WordPress supports five border settings that you can configure via the `settings.border` property in `theme.json`. Each setting allows you to enable or disable a specific border feature. Four of them accept a boolean (`true` or `false`) value, while the fifth accepts a list of objects to define border radius presets.

- `color`: Enables/Disables the border-color picker.
- `radius`: Enables/Disables the border-radius control.
- `style`: Enables/Disables the border-style selector (users can choose `solid`, `dashed`, or `dotted`).
- `width`: Enables/Disables the border-width input.
- `radiusSizes`: Defines a curated set of border radius presets that users can select from in the Block Editor.

### Default configuration
By default, the first four border properties are set to false:
```json
{
  "version": 2,
  "settings": {
    "border": {
      "color": false,
      "radius": false,
      "style": false,
      "width": false
      "radiusSizes": []
    }
  }
}
```
### Border radius presets (`radiusSizes`)
You can define border radius presets in `theme.json` under `settings.border.radiusSizes`. These presets provide consistent design values while still allowing users to enter custom values. The property accepts an array of border radius objects, each with three required properties:

- `name`: The label for your border radius preset, which will be internationalized (so that it can be translated) and shown to the user in some contexts, such as tooltips.
- `slug`: A unique machine-readable slug/ID for your border radius preset. This is used to generate CSS custom properties and CSS classes.
- `size`: A valid CSS length value (e.g., px, %).

For example, to add `None`, `Small`, `Medium`, `Large` and `Full` border radius presets:
```json
{
  "version": 3,
  "settings": {
    "border": {
      "radiusSizes": [
        {
          "name": "None",
          "slug": "none",
          "size": "0"
        },
        {
          "name": "Small",
          "slug": "small",
          "size": "4px"
        },
        {
          "name": "Medium",
          "slug": "medium",
          "size": "8px"
        },
        {
          "name": "Large",
          "slug": "large",
          "size": "16px"
        },
        {
          "name": "Full",
          "slug": "full",
          "size": "9999px"
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```
- With 1–8 presets, users see a slider with stops for each preset.
- With 9 or more presets, the control displays as a dropdown select menu.
- Users can always access custom value input through the custom button to the right of the control.
- The interface automatically adapts based on the number of presets you define.

title: [HelpHub] Clarify theme ZIP file structure for updates

labels.name: user documentation (HelpHub)
labels.description: Improvements or additions to end-user documentation

body:
The current documentation (https://wordpress.org/documentation/article/work-with-themes/#adding-new-themes-using-the-administration-screens and https://learn.wordpress.org/lesson/updating-your-theme/) implicitly assumes that a theme's ZIP file will contain a single root folder and that all theme files will reside within that folder. This is a common and well-known best practice among experienced developers. However, it is not explicitly stated as a hard requirement (or I'm unable to find this requirement in the docs).

This lack of explicit documentation can lead to a specific bug, as demonstrated in the Trac ticket https://core.trac.wordpress.org/ticket/63737. When a user attempts to update a theme via ZIP upload, if the theme's files are at the root of the ZIP archive (instead of being inside a containing folder), a previous failed update attempt (e.g., trying to upload the theme ZIP through the plugin installer) can cause subsequent, correct update attempts to fail. WordPress, in this scenario, creates a new directory (e.g., my-theme-1) instead of overwriting the existing theme folder, breaking the update process.

Proposed Change:
Add a new, clear, and prominent section to the relevant documentation that explicitly states the correct ZIP file structure for themes. This should be added to both developer-facing and user-facing documentation.
